lesson.menu_title: If I Had Known, Now I Know
lesson.menu_desc: Phase 3 -- mixed conditionals, for analysing decisions -- 38 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 22 -- If I Had Known, Now I Know -- Mixed Conditionals
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Mark Kazuyoshi Seki Omagari | Lesson 22 -- If I Had Known, Now I Know

listenings.text: Hi Mark. In lesson fourteen you learned the third conditional, where a different past gives you a different past. If I had studied, I would have passed. Both halves live in the past, and the sentence stays there. Today we break that symmetry, because real life is not symmetrical. A mixed conditional puts the two halves in different times. The first shape is the common one. The condition is in the past and the result is now. If I had taken that job, I would be living in another city today. Notice the form. If plus had plus the past participle in the first half, and would plus the bare verb in the second half. No have, no been. The second shape runs the other way. The condition is something permanent about you, and the result sits in the past. If I were more patient, I would not have said that. Here the first half is if plus the past simple, and the second half is would have plus the past participle. Both shapes exist because a decision has two lives. One is the moment you made it, and the other is the person you are because of it. Before class, think of one choice that still shapes your week, and try to say it both ways. See you on Friday, Mark.

There is one decision I keep coming back to, and it was not even a big one at the time. Two years ago my school offered a robotics club and a football team on the same afternoon, and I had about a week to choose. I chose football, because my friends were going, and because I did not want to be the only one sitting in a lab. Now, if I had joined the robotics club, I would probably be building things every weekend instead of watching other people build them online. That is the part that annoys me. The strange thing is that I do not regret playing football. I regret the reason. If I were less afraid of being the odd one out, I would not have decided it in ten seconds, and I would have asked whether I could do both. Nobody told me that was possible, and I never asked. So the trade-off was real, but it was smaller than I thought, and I paid for it in the long run. This year the club opened again. I am not going to be impulsive about it twice.

extra_audio.text: First, you name the decision itself, in the past simple, so we know what actually happened. Then you say what was at stake, so we understand why the choice was difficult. After that, you build the first mixed conditional: if plus had plus the past participle for the condition, and would plus the bare verb for the result you would be living today. Next, you turn it around with the second shape, using if plus the past simple for the thing that is permanently true about you, and would have plus the past participle for what you would have done differently. Finally, you say what you would do now, because the point of analysing a decision is the next one, not the old one.

reading.rtitle: The Ten Second Decision -- Why the Best Written Characters Choose Badly
paras: Every character you remember is remembered for a decision. Not for a fight, and not for a speech: for a moment where two doors were open and only one of them could be taken. Good writers know that the door itself is not interesting. What is interesting is how long the character stood in front of it, and what that says about who they are.

The rule most writers follow is simple. A decision that a character weighs up for three episodes is a plot point. A decision made in ten seconds is a character. Impulsive choices tell us more than careful ones, because there is no time to perform: whatever comes out is what was already there. This is why so many stories put the fatal flaw and the big choice in the same scene. If the character were patient, the story would have ended in episode two, and nobody would have watched it.

The best written decisions are also irreversible. If a door can be reopened later, the audience relaxes, and relaxed audiences stop caring. So the writer closes it: the message is sent, the ship leaves, the name is given to the wrong person. From that point the story is not about the choice anymore. It is about the version of the character that exists because of it. If she had stayed in the city, she would be a different person in season three, and the season would have nothing to say.

Which brings us to redemption, the most misused idea in television. A redemption arc is not a character apologising. It is a character being offered the same choice a second time, under the same pressure, and choosing differently. Everything before that is decoration. If the second choice costs nothing, there is no redemption, only a nice speech and a soundtrack telling you how to feel.
reading.source: The Frame -- a column on how stories are built

gist.prompt: What is this article mainly arguing?
choices: That characters who make careful decisions are better written than impulsive ones
That a decision reveals character when it is fast, irreversible, and offered again later under the same pressure
That television writers should give their characters more time to choose
